name: Qeshm Island
description: Qeshm is the largest island in the Persian Gulf, lying alongside Iran’s southern coast near the Strait of Hormuz. Its folded sedimentary landscapes, salt formations, mangroves, and maritime communities bring together geological and cultural histories. [s1][s2][s4]

seo.title: Qeshm Island: Geology, Mangroves and Maritime Heritage | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore Qeshm’s salt landscapes, coastal ecosystems and wooden-boat traditions, with distinctions between the island and its geopark designation.

content.heading: An island alongside the mainland
content.content:
Qeshm stretches roughly parallel to Iran’s southern coast, with the Khuran Strait separating it from the mainland. Its position near the entrance to the Persian Gulf helps explain why the island belongs to a wider maritime geography rather than an isolated offshore world. Encyclopaedia Iranica identifies it as the Gulf’s largest island. [s1]

The landscape also sits at a meeting point between the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman. UNESCO’s account connects that setting with a varied coastal environment that includes mangroves, coral communities, and sandy beaches. These habitats should be understood together with the island’s exposed rocks: Qeshm’s significance extends from its interior landforms to the shallow waters around it. [s2]

content.heading: Folded rocks and rising salt
content.content:
UNESCO places Qeshm at the southern edge of the Zagros mountain system, whose development reflects the collision of the Arabian and Eurasian tectonic plates. Sedimentary layers were folded, while erosion removed less resistant material and helped reveal the ridges visible today. Salt beneath the sedimentary succession contributed another kind of movement within this landscape. [s2]

Namakdan provides a particularly clear example. A salt diapir is a body of salt that has moved upward through surrounding rock. The International Union of Geological Sciences describes Namakdan as a complex containing rock salt alongside anhydrite, limestone, sandstone, shale, and volcanic material. Blocks of other rocks were carried upward with the salt. [s3]

The cave system within this formation is part of a changing landscape rather than a sealed geological monument. Research summarized by IUGS links its development to erosion, uplift, and changing sea levels. The same site also retains evidence of earlier salt and sulphur extraction and trade, connecting geological resources with human activity. [s3]

content.heading: A coast shaped by practical knowledge
content.content:
At Gouran, the geopark’s heritage account describes a traditional wooden-boat yard and a museum developed with the village community. The boats known as lenj belong to a maritime culture in which construction, repair, and sailing knowledge are closely connected. This gives the coast a human scale: harbors are workplaces as well as geographical features. [s4]

The same account describes moshta fishing, in which shore-based stakes and nets exploit the rise and fall of the tide. Fish enter with rising water and become trapped as it retreats. Such practices show how detailed knowledge of coastal rhythms can become part of everyday technology. They should not, by themselves, be treated as evidence that present fishing pressure is sustainable. [s4]

content.heading: Understanding the designation
content.content: UNESCO records 2017 as the designation year for Qeshm Island UNESCO Global Geopark. That recognition provides a framework for interpreting geological heritage; it does not replace the island’s separate identity as a place where people live and work. Reading Qeshm through both its rock formations and its maritime knowledge offers a fuller account than treating it simply as a collection of scenic stops. [s2][s4]

name: Kish Island
description: Kish is a low-lying island in the Persian Gulf with a history of maritime trade that long predates its development as a tourist destination and free trade zone. Archaeological remains at Harira and research on surrounding coral reefs reveal different dimensions of the island’s coastal setting. [s1][s2][s3]

seo.title: Kish Island: Trading History, Tourism and Coral Reefs | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Discover Kish’s medieval maritime connections, Harira’s archaeology, modern development and the limits of evidence on reef condition.

content.heading: A small island in a much larger network
content.content:
Kish lies off Iran’s southern coast in the Persian Gulf. Its generally flat terrain and historically noted palm gardens distinguish its geographical description from accounts centered on mountainous island interiors. Older sources also call it Qays, a name readers will encounter in histories of Gulf commerce. [s1]

The island rose to prominence around the middle of the eleventh century. Its rulers participated in maritime networks linking Persia, Iraq, Yemen, and India. Their origins remain uncertain: Daniel Thomas Potts’s account weighs competing traditions rather than assigning them a simple ethnic identity. This uncertainty matters because maritime communities often crossed the political and cultural boundaries used in modern descriptions. [s1]

content.heading: Harira and the material evidence of exchange
content.content:
Harira, on the island’s northern side, preserves evidence of a substantial historic settlement. Investigations described in Encyclopaedia Iranica identified buildings, boat-loading facilities, cisterns, kilns, and imported ceramics. East Asian wares connect the site’s material record with the wider exchange networks described in written sources. [s1]

Water infrastructure is another important part of this history. Cisterns and a qanat—an underground water-channel system—appear in the archaeological account. They draw attention to the practical requirements of sustaining an island settlement alongside its commercial ambitions. [s1]

content.heading: From resort planning to a free trade project
content.content:
Modern Kish reflects deliberate development policy. Arang Keshavarzian traces the free trade project to broader mid-twentieth-century debates about port congestion, infrastructure, and economic zones. Resort planning subsequently brought a different ambition: attracting business and leisure travelers through a specially developed island destination. [s2]

After the Iran–Iraq War, the project was revived within a reconstruction agenda that emphasized investment, employment, and exports. These were policy objectives, rather than proof that every intended outcome followed. The distinction helps explain why Kish should be read both as a tourism landscape and as an experiment in economic governance. Historical descriptions of incentives do not establish the rules applicable to a present-day business or visitor. [s2]

content.heading: The reef environment beneath the tourism image
content.content:
Research published in 2021 examined recreational scuba diving and coral reefs around Kish. Its abstract reports evidence of diving-related damage while describing most surveyed reefs as being in good condition under the study’s reef-health index. Those findings can coexist: an overall classification does not imply an absence of local damage. [s3]

The study concerns particular surveyed reefs and a defined investigation, so it cannot establish the condition of every Kish reef in 2026. It does, however, identify a concrete environmental dimension of tourism. A useful reading of Kish therefore holds together its archaeological record, planned development, and marine habitats, while keeping historical evidence separate from claims about present performance. [s1][s2][s3]

name: Hormuz Island
description: Hormuz Island lies near the Strait of Hormuz and is distinguished by an exposed salt dome and varied colored rocks and soils. Its northern settlement also preserves the history of a major trading port whose name originally belonged to a mainland town. [s1][s2]

seo.title: Hormuz Island: Salt Geology and a Historic Trading Port | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand Hormuz’s colored landscapes, rising salt, coastal landforms and the relocation of a mainland port to the island.

content.heading: Why the island has so many colors
content.content:
Hormuz’s colors have a geological explanation. NASA’s Earth Observatory describes the island as a salt dome: a mass containing rock salt, gypsum, anhydrite, and other evaporite minerals that has risen through overlying rocks. Under sustained pressure, salt can deform and flow rather than behave like a rigid block. [s1]

The rising material is not exclusively salt. Clay, carbonates, shale, and iron-rich volcanic rocks accompany it, with interactions involving water and minerals producing red, yellow, and orange shades. A Landsat image discussed by NASA reveals the dome’s broadly concentric structure and contrasts it with sediment-covered ground in the north. [s1]

The coast is not uniformly bare. NASA also identifies a small mangrove area at the northern end, providing habitat for fish, mollusks, crustaceans, and migratory birds. That localized wetland is an important qualification to descriptions that reduce Hormuz to colored rock and desert scenery. [s1]

content.heading: Different rocks, different shores
content.content:
A field-based study published in GeoJournal of Tourism and Geosites describes rocky and sandy shores, sea caves, salt formations, and landforms produced by differential erosion. Differential erosion means that materials wear away at different rates. On Hormuz, readily soluble salt and more resistant rocks help create pronounced contrasts in relief. [s3]

This perspective makes individual viewpoints easier to interpret: a striking cliff or valley belongs to a larger system of rock composition, dissolution, weathering, and coastal processes. The study discusses geotourism as a way to explain and preserve these features. Its suggestion that Hormuz could be developed as a geopark is a proposal, not evidence of a UNESCO designation. [s3]

content.heading: How a mainland port became an island name
content.content:
The history of Hormuz requires separating the island from Old Hormuz, a mainland port near Minab. Willem Floor’s historical account explains that insecurity led the ruler Ayaz to transfer the port community to the island then known as Jarun. The new settlement became New Hormuz; eventually the qualification disappeared and Hormuz named both town and island. [s2]

The sheltered northern harbor supported the redistribution of goods between maritime routes and smaller Gulf ports connected to inland markets. Its commercial strength depended on connections and supplies rather than agricultural self-sufficiency. The historical settlement relied on provisions brought from mainland shores and Qeshm. [s2]

In 1622, Safavid forces, assisted at sea by the English East India Company, captured Hormuz from Portuguese control. Subsequent policy favored Bandar Abbas on the mainland, and the island lost its former commercial position. This shift shows how a strategic location alone did not guarantee a port’s continuing prosperity. [s2]
